content.text:
Comment class: other
A question — answering from the review's research ([docs/declarative-checks/REVIEW.md](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/docs/declarative-checks/REVIEW.md), §2 and §6); most of its recommendations already landed in #839, so this is the remainder that's genuinely *redesign*-shaped.

**Still-open redesign recommendations from the research, ranked by value:**

1. **Fence-blind markdown scanning (textlint/remark's container suppression).** The engine blanks fenced code blocks for `checkSections`, but a plain `matchLines` rule over `.md` files can still fire on code inside a fence — the field treats "ignore matches inside code fences/links" as the *default* for prose linting, built into the engine once rather than per rule. The cleanest remaining correctness gap.
2. **A count/occurrence primitive (Vale's `occurrence`).** The bounds cluster we deliberately didn't merge: `maxLines`, `minBullets`/`maxBullets`, plus the missing "exactly N matches in scope" form that would let `scheduler-workflow-shape`'s "exactly one cron" leg convert. Pairs with the two deferred key additions in [#838](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/838) (`unlessPreviousLineMatches`, `maxLineLength`, `andLineMatches`).
3. **Fixtures as data (ESLint RuleTester's shape).** Today each declared check's fixtures are hand-written `.test.mjs`. The RuleTester model — `(input files, expected findings)` pairs as JSON beside `declared-checks.json`, run by one shared harness — would complete the checks-as-data story: declaration *and* proof both data, and "a declared check with no fixture" becomes one more meta-check leg. This is the largest structural idea left.
4. **Spectral's `@key` addressing** in `checkParsedFiles` — assert on key *names*, not values (e.g. "every key under X is kebab-case"). Noted in the review as the one capability `fieldAt` can't express; add it when a real check needs it, not before.
5. **Declarative autofix (markdownlint's `fixInfo` data-splice).** The field's two-tier fix/suggestion model, representable as pure JSON. Deliberately low priority here: our "fixer" is an agent reading the failure message, so autofix buys much less than in a human-editor linter.

**And the research's explicit *don'ts*, already settled as decisions:** no general selector algebra (JSONPath/ast-grep composition) as the base vocabulary, no inline disables (the reasoned `accept` mechanism is stronger), no tool adoption (ast-grep/Semgrep/Spectral all fail the vendored-verbatim/zero-dep constraints), and actionlint at most as an additive when-present CI layer, never a foundation.

Items 1–2 are small engine work; 3 is a real design effort; 4–5 wait for a customer.

# core

Claudinite's own surface in a repo that runs it: the vendored mount, the declaration that activates a
pack, adopting Claudinite and adopting a pack, and the contract every scheduled task is written to.

**Mandatory.** `basics` `requires` this pack, so the closure vendors its content and materializes its
declaration wherever a declaration is written; the one-time `core-seed` migration record declares it
into members that already exist. Removing the entry is not an opt-out — it is drift, and `core-declared`
reports it.

## Checks

Each of these asks the same kind of question: **is Claudinite working in this repo** — declared,
converged, gated, scheduled. A repo can fail any of them silently, which is why they are checks and
not prose: the session that has lost its rules is the session least able to notice.

| Rule | Severity | What goes wrong when it fires |
|---|---|---|
| `core-declared` | advisory | this pack's entry is gone from `.claudinite-checks.json`, so none of the rules below run and the session cannot tell |
| `rules-index-current` | blocking | the generated index is missing, stale or unimported — the repo's packs contribute no prose to any session |
| `claudinite-isolation` | blocking | the repo's own code reaches into `.claudinite/`, so the next canon refactor is a breaking migration for code the canon does not own (a declared `forbidReferences` [barrier](../barriers/README.md) edge) |
| `conformance-workflow` | advisory | nothing in CI runs the world sweep unfiltered on a pull request, so conformance is ungated and the maintenance PR never lands |
| `scheduler-workflow-shape` | blocking | the vendored scheduler's cron, concurrency or dispatch guard has drifted — staggering, double-run safety or manual runs break |
| `task-declaration-shape` | blocking | a task declaration the scheduler reads is incomplete or illegal, so the task never fires or fires wrong |
| `task-declaration-matches-folder` | blocking | a declaration disagrees with its folder — discovery drops it into `errors` and every run keeps reporting healthy without it |
| `task-phase-discipline` | advisory | a task decides not to run after its precondition already said run, hiding the decision from the run records |

The scope cuts the other way too: a rule about how the **canon's own** content is maintained is not
this pack's, however much it looks like one. `catalog-completeness` — `packs/README.md` lists every
`packs/<name>/` — reads as Claudinite machinery and is not: it can only fire in the corpus repo, and
what it guards is a hand-maintained index, not a member's status. It stays in
[basics](../basics/README.md) with the other doc-integrity rules.

## Skills

| Skill | For |
|---|---|
| [`adopt-claudinite`](skills/adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md) | setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time — mount, hooks, checks, skills — and re-baselining one to pick up updates |
| [`adopt-pack`](skills/adopt-pack/SKILL.md) | adding a pack to a repo that already runs Claudinite: declare, interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land |

`adopt-claudinite` bundles two more checks of the same kind — `adoption-answers-pending` and
`interview-answer-stale`, over the answers a member stores against each declared pack's questions.

## Tasks

| Task | frequency | Runs when |
|---|---|---|
| `adopt-requested-packs` | daily | the repo carries an open pack-adoption request |

The `update` self-refresh task is still `basics`' (`packs/basics/tasks/update/`) and moves here in a
second change, once every member's declaration is confirmed to carry `core`. A member runs that task
from its **vendored** copy, and `discoverTasks` only finds a task whose pack is literally declared —
so moving the directory before the declaration has landed everywhere would leave a member with no
update task at all, and nothing left that could deliver it one.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

1	# Declarative checks — review
2	
3	Status: review record for #838, following up #827 (declarations moved to
4	`packs/<pack>/declared-checks.json`). Covers five questions: the vocabulary's generality, message
5	discipline, what else converts, engine performance, and what the linter field teaches. The engine
6	under review is [engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs);
7	its design record is [engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md). All numbers measured
8	2026-08-14 on this checkout (610 tracked files, Node 22).
9	
10	## The short version
11	
12	- **The architecture is validated by the field.** ESLint, Vale, Spectral and markdownlint all
13	  converged on the same shapes this engine already has: rules as data over a shared single-pass
14	  scan, per-rule severity in repo config, findings that carry their own teaching text. Nothing
15	  surveyed is adoptable as a dependency under the vendored-verbatim / zero-dependency constraints —
16	  the win is importing idioms, and several of the best are already here (Vale's document-part
17	  scoping ≈ `checkSections`; Spectral's `given`/`then` ≈ the parsed-doc assertions).
18	- **Generality**: 10 of the 18 spec keys are single-use — the per-case reading is right for the
19	  long tail. Three key clusters are the same idea spelled thrice and can merge; four cross-rule
20	  facilities (named file classes, structural self-exclusion, a rule-level `fix` default,
21	  comment-blind scanning) would remove most of the boilerplate that makes declarations long.
22	- **Messages**: the median message field is 16 words but the tail runs to 58; fix strings restate
23	  whole policies and repeat verbatim within rules. The field's discipline — quote the evidence,
24	  state one action — plus a meta-check over the spec files themselves (the format is JSON, so the
25	  meta-lint is a schema plus word caps, itself landable as a declared check) closes it.
26	- **Conversion**: 5 of 61 imperative code rules convert today with zero vocabulary change (the five
27	  jwt rules — one shared mechanism, ~220 lines to delete); ~5 more with three genuinely general
28	  key additions. The other ~50 stay imperative for structural reasons (git state, session
29	  transcript, config-driven scans, real parsing, cross-file joins). The bigger cleanup there is
30	  helper consolidation: four copies of comment-stripping, three hand-rolled config-schema
31	  validators, three base-vs-head JSON key diffs.
32	- **Performance**: the whole-repo world sweep is 0.67s; the declarative engine is already the fast
33	  path (all 25 declared rules share one ~35ms scan). The two real boosts are the `barrier` rule
34	  (274ms — 61% of rule time, re-extracting per-line candidates once per edge) and the base-ref
35	  refresh fetch (0.7–8s of network per run, paid again on every Stop-hook turn with changes).
36	
37	## 1. The measured state
38	
39	89 registered rules across canon + local packs: 25 pattern-declared (JSON), 3 barrier edges
40	declared as pack-manifest data (a second, older declarative vocabulary), 61 imperative code rules.
41	All 13 work-scoped rules are imperative — `patternRule` has no work-scope vocabulary (nothing over
42	added lines, commits, or the transcript), so every declared check is world-scoped by construction.
43	
44	Key usage across the 25 declarations: `matchLines` 6, `checkEachFile` 5, `checkSections` 5,
45	`relevantWhen` 5 — the workhorses — then a long tail of one use each: `maxLines`,
46	`coveredByGlobLine`, `listedInFile`, `checkKeyValueFile`, `equalParsedValues`, `requirePaths`,
47	`whenMissing`, `checkParsedFile`, `forEachParsedEntry`, `repoWide`, `skipLinesMatching`.
48	
49	Whole-repo world sweep (35 active world rules on the home): 0.67s wall without the base-ref fetch,
50	1.43s with it. Phase split: module imports 22ms, pack discovery 44ms, context build 42ms, rules
51	452ms. Slowest rules: `barrier` 274ms, `pack-discovery-entry-await` 55ms, the entire declared-rule
52	family ~35ms (billed to whichever declared rule runs first — the shared-scan design working as
53	intended), `warning-suppression` 24ms, `markdown-link-labels` 12ms.
54	
55	## 2. Generality (task 1)
56	
57	The per-case shape is real but concentrated: the workhorse keys are genuinely general, and the
58	long tail is one key per converted check. Three clusters are the same idea under different names
59	and can collapse without inventing a query language:
60	
61	| Cluster | Keys today | One idea |
62	|---|---|---|
63	| Bounds | `maxLines`; `minBullets`/`maxBullets`/`maxBulletBlockLength` (inside `checkSections`) | a count/length bound over a unit (lines, bullets, characters) |
64	| Index coverage | `listedInFile`, `coveredByGlobLine` | every selected path must be covered by an entry in an index file — the two differ only in what an entry is (an `asText` template vs a first-token glob) |
65	| Parsed-document assertions | `checkParsedFile`, `forEachParsedEntry`, `equalParsedValues` | select nodes by field path (with filters), then assert — Spectral's `given`/`then`, already backed by one shared parse cache and `fieldAt` |
66	
67	The parsed-document merge is the highest-value one: a `checkParsedFiles` entry with a field-path
68	selector (`inFilesMatching`/`file` + `atField` + `whereFieldEquals`) and a small closed assertion
69	set (`requireField`, `forbidField`, `forbidValueInArray`, `equalsFieldIn` another file) carries all
70	three current keys plus the next several structured checks, and message placeholders (`{path}`,
71	`{value}`) fall out of the selector. Spectral's `@key` addressing (assert on key names, not
72	values) is the one missing capability the current `fieldAt` model can't express.
73	
74	Two consolidations are cheaper than they look and remove more authoring friction than any key
75	merge — the boilerplate is what actually makes declarations read as verbose:
76	
77	- **Named file classes.** `excludeFiles` regexes for test files are hand-repeated
78	  (`google-token-email-verified`, `web-speech-capture-released-on-pagehide` carry near-identical
79	  test/fixture exclusions), and every skill's checks hand-exclude the skill's own directory
80	  (`"excludeFiles": "/^skills\\/google-id-token-validation\\//"`). Named classes usable at
81	  `scanFiles`/`excludeFiles` (`"testFiles"`, `"codeFiles"`, `"workflowFiles"`) mirror Vale's
82	  scopes and ESLint's shared settings; the self-exclusion shouldn't even be a class — the engine
83	  knows which directory a declaration file lives in, so excluding the declaring skill's own tree is
84	  structural (the canon's own prefer-structural-classifier rule, applied to the engine).
85	- **Rule-level message defaults.** `in-session-github-access` repeats one 30-word `fix` three
86	  times; `product-wiki-growth-log` repeats its fix three times. A rule-level `fix` (and `what`)
87	  default inherited by assertions, overridable per assertion, removes the duplication the
88	  format's no-comments rule otherwise amplifies.
89	
90	And one capability gap: the imperative side has string-aware comment stripping
91	([engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs](../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs)); the
92	declarative side only has `skipLinesMatching`, which `in-session-github-access` uses as a weaker
93	approximation (`/^\s*(\/\/|\*|\/\*)/` misses trailing comments and can match inside strings). A
94	`scanIgnoringComments: true` key backed by `stripComments` (newline-preserving, so line numbers
95	hold) makes the declarative form as precise as the code it replaces — and is a precondition for
96	converting most code-facing candidates.
97	
98	What NOT to do: a general selector algebra (JSONPath, ast-grep's `all`/`any`/`not`/`inside`
99	composition) as the base vocabulary. The corpus's own rulings decide this — keys must read alone
100	to a cold reader (#789/#799), and a knob nobody would set differently shouldn't exist (#707). The
101	composition vocabulary is the growth path *when a real check needs it*, added as wordy named keys,
102	not a platform to build ahead of need. Single-use keys whose semantics are genuinely distinct
103	(`checkKeyValueFile`, `repoWide`) are fine as they are: each is data over shared machinery, and
104	deleting them buys nothing.
105	
106	## 3. Message discipline (task 2)
107	
108	A declared check's failure renders `what` + `failureMessage` (as the why line) + `fix`. Median
109	field is 16 words; the tail: `web-speech-capture-released-on-pagehide.fix` 58 words,
110	`google-token-email-verified.failureMessage` 47, `gha/no-scheduled-fleet-executor.fix` 44,
111	`product-wiki-freshness.fix` 40 (with an embedded JSON snippet). The long ones share a shape:
112	`failureMessage` argues the rule's philosophy in multiple clauses, and `fix` restates the whole
113	policy including its alternatives instead of naming the one action.
114	
115	The surveyed tools converge on a tight message discipline (ESLint's ecosystem enforces
116	`^[A-Z].*\.$` — a complete sentence stating the problem; Semgrep interpolates the matched text into
117	the message; Vale caps a message at what the writer must do):
118	
119	- **`what` quotes the evidence.** State the violated expectation with the matched content in it —
120	  the engine's `{match}`/`{path}`/capture-group interpolation exists; use it everywhere. A finding
121	  that quotes the offending token is actionable; one that restates the rule is not.
122	- **`fix` is one imperative clause** — the single next action. Alternatives, escape hatches, and
123	  policy context are the `failureMessage`'s one causal clause or nothing. When a fix wants a menu,
124	  that's usually the rule doing two jobs (or prose that belongs in the pack's README).
125	- **`failureMessage` is the consequence, once** — why the defect bites, ≤ ~20 words. Where `what`
126	  already implies it, shorter still. (It doubles as the catalog description in `--list`, which
127	  rewards the one-line form.)
128	- **Enforce it with a meta-check.** The format being JSON makes this cheap and is the field's
129	  "lint the linter" idiom (`eslint-plugin-eslint-plugin`): a declared check over
130	  `packs/*/declared-checks.json` — word caps per field, no fix string repeated verbatim within a
131	  rule (that's the rule-level default's job), interpolation keys that exist. The existing
132	  vocabulary can carry the word caps today; the rest is a small imperative check or a schema.
133	
134	Fixture discipline transfers too: ESLint's RuleTester contract — every rule tested as
135	(input text, expected findings) pairs through the real engine, every message exercised — is the
136	see-it-fail rule in executable form, and
137	[engine-tests/pattern-rules.test.mjs](../../engine-tests/pattern-rules.test.mjs) already runs that
138	way. Worth pinning as the convention when the meta-check lands: a declared check with no fixture
139	exercising it is a finding.
140	
141	## 4. What else converts (task 3)
142	
143	Full per-rule audit: 61 imperative code rules (plus one CLI-only gate and the 3 barrier-data
144	edges). Verdicts:
145	
146	**Convertible now, zero vocabulary change — 5 rules, one cluster.** The five jwt rules
147	(`jwt-hardcoded-secret`, `jwt-sign-sets-expiry`, `jwt-none-not-accepted`,
148	`jwt-verify-binds-audience`, `jwt-verify-pins-algorithms`) are all the same mechanism: select
149	non-test source files → gate on the file importing the library → optionally bail on a word
150	appearing anywhere in the file → flag lines matching a call pattern. That is exactly
151	`scanFiles` + `excludeFiles` + `whenFileMatches` + `unlessFileMatches` + `matchLines`. Converting
152	them deletes ~220 lines plus the pack's `scan.mjs` and is the single best next conversion.
153	(Partial conversions also available now: `product-wiki-layout`'s `requirePaths` half,
154	`skill-no-enforcement-narration`'s runner-mention half.)
155	
156	**Convertible with a small, genuinely general extension — ~5 rules.** Ranked by the #707 test
157	(who else would use the key):
158	
159	| Extension | Carries | General? |
160	|---|---|---|
161	| `unlessPreviousLineMatches` on a matchLines assertion | `warning-suppression` (reason-above-the-marker) | yes — previous-line context is a standard line-scan concept |
162	| `maxLineLength` (bytes) beside `maxLines` | `rules-line-length` | yes — every prose-width rule |
163	| `andLineMatches` (second must-also-match pattern) | `task-phase-discipline` | yes — conjunction on one line |
164	| whole-text multiline match (`matchText`) | `sudden-termination-vs-teardown` | borderline — one user today |
165	| match-count / numeric-capture range | `scheduler-workflow-shape`'s cron legs | borderline — Vale's `occurrence` says the count form recurs; the numeric range is one user |
166	
167	A key added for exactly one rule reproduces the per-case smell — the borderline two should wait
168	for a second customer.
169	
170	**Stays imperative — ~50 rules**, for causes the vocabulary shouldn't chase: git history/diff/base
171	state (14 — all work-scoped rules among them), session transcript (3), project/pack config driving
172	the scan (9), pack metadata via `ctx.packs` (5), real parsing — balanced brackets, indentation
173	state, HTML attributes, TOML (16), cross-file joins where one file's parsed value names the other
174	(8). A declarative work scope (assertions over added lines) would cover only ~3 rules today — not
175	worth the vocabulary until that changes.
176	
177	**The cheaper wins in the imperative corpus are consolidations, not conversions:**
178	
179	- Four separate comment-stripping implementations (`code-scanning.mjs`'s, leaflet's
180	  length-preserving fork, and two local-pack copies) → one helper with a `preserveOffsets` option.
181	- Three hand-rolled pack-entry config validators (`growth-config`, `preferences-store-configured`,
182	  `barrier`'s config half) → one declarative config-schema seam on the pack manifest (ESLint's
183	  `meta.schema` idiom).
184	- Three base-vs-head JSON key diffs (`node/earn-each-dependency`, `cer/permission-added-store-issue`,
185	  `adoption-answers-pending`) → a `work.addedKeys(file, atPath)` helper.
186	- The near-identical `cer/release-workflows` / `sw/release-workflows` pair → shared
187	  "vendored set present" machinery, with the `requirePaths` halves declarable today.
188	
189	## 5. The engine, and the quick performance boost (task 4)
190	
191	The mechanism is sound: one pass over the scanned tree for every pattern rule, per-context result
192	cache, shared read and parse caches, lines split once per file per pass. At 25 declared rules the
193	whole family costs ~35ms — adding declared rules is nearly free, which is the property the
194	conversion program needs. Two boosts are worth taking; both are localized:
195	
196	1. **The `barrier` scan re-derives per-line candidates once per edge** (274ms, 61% of rule time).
197	   the barrier engine (at review time `packs/barriers/engine.mjs`; since moved to
198	   [engine/checks/helpers/reference-scanning.mjs](../../engine/checks/helpers/reference-scanning.mjs))
199	   runs `candidatesOn(line)` (two
200	   regex sweeps) and `resolveRef` per candidate inside `scanEdge`, so a `siblings` edge — expanded
201	   to one sub-edge per child directory — and any overlapping edges recompute identical extraction.
202	   Candidates depend only on the line; caching extraction per file (as the pattern engine caches
203	   its scan per context) makes edge count nearly free. A cheap prefilter (skip lines containing
204	   neither `.` nor `/`) stacks on top. Expected: most of the 274ms on multi-edge repos.
205	2. **The base-ref refresh fetch is the dominant wall-clock item** (~0.75s here, up to its 8s
206	   timeout; `refreshBaseRef` in
207	   [engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs](../../engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs)) — and
208	   the Stop hook pays it on every turn with tracked changes. The fetch exists for work-scope
209	   honesty (the stale-base false-verdict class DESIGN.md documents) and must stay; the boost is a
210	   freshness window —
211	   skip the fetch when the remote-tracking ref was already refreshed within the last few minutes
212	   (readable from `FETCH_HEAD`/ref mtime). Bounded staleness, no correctness change beyond the
213	   window, and it converts the per-turn cost to once per session burst. (Skipping the fetch
214	   entirely in world-`all` runs is tempting but wrong to do blind: `--changed` scoping and the
215	   delta context still derive from the merge-base.)
216	
217	Not worth taking: the per-file `existsSync`+`statSync` pair and the ~10 git spawns in context
218	build (42ms total), and pack discovery's eager imports (44ms — load-bearing for structural
219	discovery, #581).
220	
221	## 6. Technology review (task 5)
222	
223	Constraints that frame every verdict: plain Node ≥18, zero dependencies, the engine vendored
224	verbatim into members, everything must run on credentials and settings members already have. A
225	tool members must install is dead-on-arrival per the standing ruling (a missing binary = the
226	capability silently dead per repo); a native-binary npm dependency breaks vendored-verbatim.
227	
228	### The tools
229	
230	| Tool | What it is | Verdict for us |
231	|---|---|---|
232	| **ESLint v10** | JS linter; since v9.7 a language-agnostic core with official JSON/Markdown/CSS language plugins — rules are `{meta, create}` listeners over a shared parse | Not adoptable (JS-ecosystem dependency tree), but the strongest source of idioms: `meta.messages` with `{{placeholders}}`, `meta.schema` validating per-rule options, capability flags (`fixable`, `hasSuggestions`), RuleTester's valid/invalid contract, and meta-linting rules themselves. Its `no-restricted-syntax` — a generic engine rule instanced by per-config selector+message data — is the field's endorsement of exactly the `patternRule` design (and its findings all reporting one shared rule id is the weakness our per-spec `id` already avoids) |
233	| **ast-grep** | Rust/tree-sitter structural search; YAML rules (`pattern`/`kind`/`regex` atoms, `inside`/`has` relations, `all`/`any`/`not` composition); Node via `@ast-grep/napi` | **Poor fit.** Our targets are Markdown prose, YAML workflows, JSON configs — Markdown isn't a built-in language (custom grammar = per-platform native artifact), plain text isn't a language at all, and napi is a 0.x native addon resolving nine platform-specific binaries. For config files, path-shaped queries (Spectral) beat CST compositions. Steal the rule-file vocabulary (`id/message/severity/note/fix`, named `utils` sub-rules, the composition algebra) as a future growth path, not the tool |
234	| **Semgrep** | OCaml/Python semantic grep; `patterns`/`pattern-either`/`pattern-not-inside`, metavariables interpolated into messages; `generic` mode for config-ish text | Non-embeddable (no Node surface; CLI install per member) and the official rules are under an internal-use-only license. Steal: AND/OR/not-inside vocabulary, metavariable-in-message, `focus-metavariable` (match wide, report narrow), per-rule `paths.include/exclude` |
235	| **remark-lint / markdownlint / textlint** | Markdown/prose linters over mdast / micromark tokens / TxtAST | The dependency trees don't transfer; the contracts do. markdownlint hands every rule both the token stream *and* raw `lines` — endorsement of our line-first engine with an optional structural layer (which `checkSections` already is). Its `fixInfo` (`{lineNumber, editColumn, deleteCount, insertText}` — a fix as a data splice) is the most vendorable autofix model surveyed, the natural shape if declared checks ever grow fixes. Container suppression (ignore matches inside code fences) should be engine-default — `markdownIndex` already blanks fences for sections; line rules don't get that for free yet |
236	| **Vale** | Go prose linter: styles = directories of YAML rules, each `extends` one of 11 closed primitives (`existence`, `occurrence`, `substitution`, …), with `scope:` targeting document parts (heading/paragraph/list/code) | The closest architectural cousin, independently converged: closed primitive set instantiated by data ≈ the assertion vocabulary; `scope` ≈ `checkSections`. Its `occurrence` primitive (min/max matches in scope) confirms the bounds-cluster merge in §2; single-binary Go distribution confirms there's no free lunch for prose linting as a dependency |
237	| **Spectral** | Node JSON/YAML linter: `given` (JSONPath) selects nodes, `then` (`field` + function from a small closed set: `pattern`, `truthy`, `defined`, `schema`, `enumeration`, `length`) asserts; `{{path}}`/`{{value}}` message placeholders; `@key` addresses key names | ~20 runtime dependencies — not adoptable. The `given`/`then` decomposition is the model for the parsed-document merge in §2, implementable as a dot-path subset over the existing `fieldAt` + [minimal-yaml](../../engine/checks/helpers/minimal-yaml.mjs) machinery (the YAML half the field solves with heavy parsers, this engine already solved with a vendored minimal one) |
238	| **actionlint / yamllint** | Deep GitHub-workflow checker (typed `${{ }}` expression checking against modeled contexts) / YAML style checker | actionlint's depth comes from modeling the platform's types — beyond our economics to build, wrong to imitate with regexes. The defensible integration is additive-when-present: a member CI step, or invoked only if the binary exists with an explicit "tool absent, skipped" note (never silent). yamllint: closed rule set, notable only as severity/inline-disable prior art |
239	
240	### Cross-cutting idioms worth importing
241	
242	Beyond the ones already folded into §§2–3 (message discipline, meta-lint, named scopes, rule-level
243	defaults, fixture contract):
244	
245	- **Dual-tier remediation** — auto-applied `fix` vs human-opted `suggestion`, declared as a
246	  capability in rule metadata. Relevant only if declared checks grow fixes; if they do,
247	  markdownlint's data-splice shape keeps the spec pure JSON.
248	- **Rule tags** for bulk toggling (markdownlint's `headings`/`whitespace`; Semgrep categories).
249	  At 89 rules with per-pack activation already doing most of that job, not yet earned.
250	- **`off` as a severity value** — already exists (`rules: {"<id>": "off"}`); the field confirms
251	  one-knob-per-rule over separate disable mechanisms.
252	- **Inline disables** (the five-verb `disable`/`enable`/`disable-line`/`disable-next-line`/
253	  configure-file grammar, with required reasons). The config-side `accept` mechanism with
254	  mandatory reasons is deliberately stronger (reviewable in one file, provenance-stamped);
255	  importing inline disables would weaken it. Noted to reject explicitly.
256	- **A doc URL riding in the finding** (`meta.docs.url`, Vale `link`): the surveyed tools carry
257	  one; #827 settled that declarations are self-standing, and the message discipline in §3 is how
258	  that stays workable.
259	
260	### Embeddability conclusion
261	
262	Four options weighed: keep the hand-rolled engine (zero install surface, and the hard parts of the
263	big tools — JS ASTs, taint analysis, typed workflow contexts — are parts this corpus doesn't
264	need); depend on `@ast-grep/napi` (native 0.x addon, nine platform binaries — breaks
265	vendored-verbatim for no Markdown/prose payoff); shell out to member-installed CLIs (violates the
266	runs-on-what-members-have ruling; Semgrep adds a rules-licensing hazard); or adopt formats without
267	tools. **The last, on top of the first, wins on every axis** — and is what §§2–5 spell out
268	concretely.
269	
270	## Sources
271	
272	Primary: this tree (engine, packs, tests) and the measurements in §1/§5. External, read
273	2026-08-14: [ESLint custom rules](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/extend/custom-rules),
274	[no-restricted-syntax](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/rules/no-restricted-syntax),
275	[languages](https://eslint.org/docs/latest/extend/languages),
276	[eslint-plugin-eslint-plugin](https://github.com/eslint-community/eslint-plugin-eslint-plugin),
277	[ast-grep rule config](https://ast-grep.github.io/guide/rule-config.html),
278	[ast-grep languages](https://ast-grep.github.io/reference/languages.html),
279	[ast-grep JS API](https://ast-grep.github.io/guide/api-usage/js-api.html),
280	[Semgrep rule syntax](https://docs.semgrep.dev/writing-rules/rule-syntax),
281	[Semgrep generic mode](https://docs.semgrep.dev/writing-rules/generic-pattern-matching),
282	[Semgrep licensing](https://docs.semgrep.dev/licensing),
283	[markdownlint custom rules](https://github.com/DavidAnson/markdownlint/blob/main/doc/CustomRules.md),
284	[remark-lint](https://github.com/remarkjs/remark-lint),
285	[textlint rule docs](https://github.com/textlint/textlint/blob/master/docs/rule.md),
286	[Vale styles](https://docs.vale.sh/topics/styles),
287	[Spectral rulesets](https://docs.stoplight.io/docs/spectral/e5b9616d6d50c-rulesets),
288	[actionlint](https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint),
289	[yamllint rules](https://yamllint.readthedocs.io/en/stable/rules.html). Versions via the npm
290	registry API. Unverified (flagged, not asserted): Semgrep's install channels; whether Semgrep
291	still accepts the legacy INFO/WARNING/ERROR severities; `@ast-grep/napi` support for custom
292	tree-sitter grammars.

# Declarative checks — review

Status: review record for #838, following up #827 (declarations moved to
`packs/<pack>/declared-checks.json`). Covers five questions: the vocabulary's generality, message
discipline, what else converts, engine performance, and what the linter field teaches. The engine
under review is [engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs](../../engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs);
its design record is [engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md). All numbers measured
2026-08-14 on this checkout (610 tracked files, Node 22).

## The short version

- **The architecture is validated by the field.** ESLint, Vale, Spectral and markdownlint all
  converged on the same shapes this engine already has: rules as data over a shared single-pass
  scan, per-rule severity in repo config, findings that carry their own teaching text. Nothing
  surveyed is adoptable as a dependency under the vendored-verbatim / zero-dependency constraints —
  the win is importing idioms, and several of the best are already here (Vale's document-part
  scoping ≈ `checkSections`; Spectral's `given`/`then` ≈ the parsed-doc assertions).
- **Generality**: 10 of the 18 spec keys are single-use — the per-case reading is right for the
  long tail. Three key clusters are the same idea spelled thrice and can merge; four cross-rule
  facilities (named file classes, structural self-exclusion, a rule-level `fix` default,
  comment-blind scanning) would remove most of the boilerplate that makes declarations long.
- **Messages**: the median message field is 16 words but the tail runs to 58; fix strings restate
  whole policies and repeat verbatim within rules. The field's discipline — quote the evidence,
  state one action — plus a meta-check over the spec files themselves (the format is JSON, so the
  meta-lint is a schema plus word caps, itself landable as a declared check) closes it.
- **Conversion**: 5 of 61 imperative code rules convert today with zero vocabulary change (the five
  jwt rules — one shared mechanism, ~220 lines to delete); ~5 more with three genuinely general
  key additions. The other ~50 stay imperative for structural reasons (git state, session
  transcript, config-driven scans, real parsing, cross-file joins). The bigger cleanup there is
  helper consolidation: four copies of comment-stripping, three hand-rolled config-schema
  validators, three base-vs-head JSON key diffs.
- **Performance**: the whole-repo world sweep is 0.67s; the declarative engine is already the fast
  path (all 25 declared rules share one ~35ms scan). The two real boosts are the `barrier` rule
  (274ms — 61% of rule time, re-extracting per-line candidates once per edge) and the base-ref
  refresh fetch (0.7–8s of network per run, paid again on every Stop-hook turn with changes).

## 1. The measured state

89 registered rules across canon + local packs: 25 pattern-declared (JSON), 3 barrier edges
declared as pack-manifest data (a second, older declarative vocabulary), 61 imperative code rules.
All 13 work-scoped rules are imperative — `patternRule` has no work-scope vocabulary (nothing over
added lines, commits, or the transcript), so every declared check is world-scoped by construction.

Key usage across the 25 declarations: `matchLines` 6, `checkEachFile` 5, `checkSections` 5,
`relevantWhen` 5 — the workhorses — then a long tail of one use each: `maxLines`,
`coveredByGlobLine`, `listedInFile`, `checkKeyValueFile`, `equalParsedValues`, `requirePaths`,
`whenMissing`, `checkParsedFile`, `forEachParsedEntry`, `repoWide`, `skipLinesMatching`.

Whole-repo world sweep (35 active world rules on the home): 0.67s wall without the base-ref fetch,
1.43s with it. Phase split: module imports 22ms, pack discovery 44ms, context build 42ms, rules
452ms. Slowest rules: `barrier` 274ms, `pack-discovery-entry-await` 55ms, the entire declared-rule
family ~35ms (billed to whichever declared rule runs first — the shared-scan design working as
intended), `warning-suppression` 24ms, `markdown-link-labels` 12ms.

## 2. Generality (task 1)

The per-case shape is real but concentrated: the workhorse keys are genuinely general, and the
long tail is one key per converted check. Three clusters are the same idea under different names
and can collapse without inventing a query language:

| Cluster | Keys today | One idea |
|---|---|---|
| Bounds | `maxLines`; `minBullets`/`maxBullets`/`maxBulletBlockLength` (inside `checkSections`) | a count/length bound over a unit (lines, bullets, characters) |
| Index coverage | `listedInFile`, `coveredByGlobLine` | every selected path must be covered by an entry in an index file — the two differ only in what an entry is (an `asText` template vs a first-token glob) |
| Parsed-document assertions | `checkParsedFile`, `forEachParsedEntry`, `equalParsedValues` | select nodes by field path (with filters), then assert — Spectral's `given`/`then`, already backed by one shared parse cache and `fieldAt` |

The parsed-document merge is the highest-value one: a `checkParsedFiles` entry with a field-path
selector (`inFilesMatching`/`file` + `atField` + `whereFieldEquals`) and a small closed assertion
set (`requireField`, `forbidField`, `forbidValueInArray`, `equalsFieldIn` another file) carries all
three current keys plus the next several structured checks, and message placeholders (`{path}`,
`{value}`) fall out of the selector. Spectral's `@key` addressing (assert on key names, not
values) is the one missing capability the current `fieldAt` model can't express.

Two consolidations are cheaper than they look and remove more authoring friction than any key
merge — the boilerplate is what actually makes declarations read as verbose:

- **Named file classes.** `excludeFiles` regexes for test files are hand-repeated
  (`google-token-email-verified`, `web-speech-capture-released-on-pagehide` carry near-identical
  test/fixture exclusions), and every skill's checks hand-exclude the skill's own directory
  (`"excludeFiles": "/^skills\\/google-id-token-validation\\//"`). Named classes usable at
  `scanFiles`/`excludeFiles` (`"testFiles"`, `"codeFiles"`, `"workflowFiles"`) mirror Vale's
  scopes and ESLint's shared settings; the self-exclusion shouldn't even be a class — the engine
  knows which directory a declaration file lives in, so excluding the declaring skill's own tree is
  structural (the canon's own prefer-structural-classifier rule, applied to the engine).
- **Rule-level message defaults.** `in-session-github-access` repeats one 30-word `fix` three
  times; `product-wiki-growth-log` repeats its fix three times. A rule-level `fix` (and `what`)
  default inherited by assertions, overridable per assertion, removes the duplication the
  format's no-comments rule otherwise amplifies.

And one capability gap: the imperative side has string-aware comment stripping
([engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs](../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs)); the
declarative side only has `skipLinesMatching`, which `in-session-github-access` uses as a weaker
approximation (`/^\s*(\/\/|\*|\/\*)/` misses trailing comments and can match inside strings). A
`scanIgnoringComments: true` key backed by `stripComments` (newline-preserving, so line numbers
hold) makes the declarative form as precise as the code it replaces — and is a precondition for
converting most code-facing candidates.

What NOT to do: a general selector algebra (JSONPath, ast-grep's `all`/`any`/`not`/`inside`
composition) as the base vocabulary. The corpus's own rulings decide this — keys must read alone
to a cold reader (#789/#799), and a knob nobody would set differently shouldn't exist (#707). The
composition vocabulary is the growth path *when a real check needs it*, added as wordy named keys,
not a platform to build ahead of need. Single-use keys whose semantics are genuinely distinct
(`checkKeyValueFile`, `repoWide`) are fine as they are: each is data over shared machinery, and
deleting them buys nothing.

## 3. Message discipline (task 2)

A declared check's failure renders `what` + `failureMessage` (as the why line) + `fix`. Median
field is 16 words; the tail: `web-speech-capture-released-on-pagehide.fix` 58 words,
`google-token-email-verified.failureMessage` 47, `gha/no-scheduled-fleet-executor.fix` 44,
`product-wiki-freshness.fix` 40 (with an embedded JSON snippet). The long ones share a shape:
`failureMessage` argues the rule's philosophy in multiple clauses, and `fix` restates the whole
policy including its alternatives instead of naming the one action.

The surveyed tools converge on a tight message discipline (ESLint's ecosystem enforces
`^[A-Z].*\.$` — a complete sentence stating the problem; Semgrep interpolates the matched text into
the message; Vale caps a message at what the writer must do):

- **`what` quotes the evidence.** State the violated expectation with the matched content in it —
  the engine's `{match}`/`{path}`/capture-group interpolation exists; use it everywhere. A finding
  that quotes the offending token is actionable; one that restates the rule is not.
- **`fix` is one imperative clause** — the single next action. Alternatives, escape hatches, and
  policy context are the `failureMessage`'s one causal clause or nothing. When a fix wants a menu,
  that's usually the rule doing two jobs (or prose that belongs in the pack's README).
- **`failureMessage` is the consequence, once** — why the defect bites, ≤ ~20 words. Where `what`
  already implies it, shorter still. (It doubles as the catalog description in `--list`, which
  rewards the one-line form.)
- **Enforce it with a meta-check.** The format being JSON makes this cheap and is the field's
  "lint the linter" idiom (`eslint-plugin-eslint-plugin`): a declared check over
  `packs/*/declared-checks.json` — word caps per field, no fix string repeated verbatim within a
  rule (that's the rule-level default's job), interpolation keys that exist. The existing
  vocabulary can carry the word caps today; the rest is a small imperative check or a schema.

Fixture discipline transfers too: ESLint's RuleTester contract — every rule tested as
(input text, expected findings) pairs through the real engine, every message exercised — is the
see-it-fail rule in executable form, and
[engine-tests/pattern-rules.test.mjs](../../engine-tests/pattern-rules.test.mjs) already runs that
way. Worth pinning as the convention when the meta-check lands: a declared check with no fixture
exercising it is a finding.

## 4. What else converts (task 3)

Full per-rule audit: 61 imperative code rules (plus one CLI-only gate and the 3 barrier-data
edges). Verdicts:

**Convertible now, zero vocabulary change — 5 rules, one cluster.** The five jwt rules
(`jwt-hardcoded-secret`, `jwt-sign-sets-expiry`, `jwt-none-not-accepted`,
`jwt-verify-binds-audience`, `jwt-verify-pins-algorithms`) are all the same mechanism: select
non-test source files → gate on the file importing the library → optionally bail on a word
appearing anywhere in the file → flag lines matching a call pattern. That is exactly
`scanFiles` + `excludeFiles` + `whenFileMatches` + `unlessFileMatches` + `matchLines`. Converting
them deletes ~220 lines plus the pack's `scan.mjs` and is the single best next conversion.
(Partial conversions also available now: `product-wiki-layout`'s `requirePaths` half,
`skill-no-enforcement-narration`'s runner-mention half.)

**Convertible with a small, genuinely general extension — ~5 rules.** Ranked by the #707 test
(who else would use the key):

| Extension | Carries | General? |
|---|---|---|
| `unlessPreviousLineMatches` on a matchLines assertion | `warning-suppression` (reason-above-the-marker) | yes — previous-line context is a standard line-scan concept |
| `maxLineLength` (bytes) beside `maxLines` | `rules-line-length` | yes — every prose-width rule |
| `andLineMatches` (second must-also-match pattern) | `task-phase-discipline` | yes — conjunction on one line |
| whole-text multiline match (`matchText`) | `sudden-termination-vs-teardown` | borderline — one user today |
| match-count / numeric-capture range | `scheduler-workflow-shape`'s cron legs | borderline — Vale's `occurrence` says the count form recurs; the numeric range is one user |

A key added for exactly one rule reproduces the per-case smell — the borderline two should wait
for a second customer.

**Stays imperative — ~50 rules**, for causes the vocabulary shouldn't chase: git history/diff/base
state (14 — all work-scoped rules among them), session transcript (3), project/pack config driving
the scan (9), pack metadata via `ctx.packs` (5), real parsing — balanced brackets, indentation
state, HTML attributes, TOML (16), cross-file joins where one file's parsed value names the other
(8). A declarative work scope (assertions over added lines) would cover only ~3 rules today — not
worth the vocabulary until that changes.

**The cheaper wins in the imperative corpus are consolidations, not conversions:**

- Four separate comment-stripping implementations (`code-scanning.mjs`'s, leaflet's
  length-preserving fork, and two local-pack copies) → one helper with a `preserveOffsets` option.
- Three hand-rolled pack-entry config validators (`growth-config`, `preferences-store-configured`,
  `barrier`'s config half) → one declarative config-schema seam on the pack manifest (ESLint's
  `meta.schema` idiom).
- Three base-vs-head JSON key diffs (`node/earn-each-dependency`, `cer/permission-added-store-issue`,
  `adoption-answers-pending`) → a `work.addedKeys(file, atPath)` helper.
- The near-identical `cer/release-workflows` / `sw/release-workflows` pair → shared
  "vendored set present" machinery, with the `requirePaths` halves declarable today.

## 5. The engine, and the quick performance boost (task 4)

The mechanism is sound: one pass over the scanned tree for every pattern rule, per-context result
cache, shared read and parse caches, lines split once per file per pass. At 25 declared rules the
whole family costs ~35ms — adding declared rules is nearly free, which is the property the
conversion program needs. Two boosts are worth taking; both are localized:

1. **The `barrier` scan re-derives per-line candidates once per edge** (274ms, 61% of rule time).
   the barrier engine (at review time `packs/barriers/engine.mjs`; since moved to
   [engine/checks/helpers/reference-scanning.mjs](../../engine/checks/helpers/reference-scanning.mjs))
   runs `candidatesOn(line)` (two
   regex sweeps) and `resolveRef` per candidate inside `scanEdge`, so a `siblings` edge — expanded
   to one sub-edge per child directory — and any overlapping edges recompute identical extraction.
   Candidates depend only on the line; caching extraction per file (as the pattern engine caches
   its scan per context) makes edge count nearly free. A cheap prefilter (skip lines containing
   neither `.` nor `/`) stacks on top. Expected: most of the 274ms on multi-edge repos.
2. **The base-ref refresh fetch is the dominant wall-clock item** (~0.75s here, up to its 8s
   timeout; `refreshBaseRef` in
   [engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs](../../engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs)) — and
   the Stop hook pays it on every turn with tracked changes. The fetch exists for work-scope
   honesty (the stale-base false-verdict class DESIGN.md documents) and must stay; the boost is a
   freshness window —
   skip the fetch when the remote-tracking ref was already refreshed within the last few minutes
   (readable from `FETCH_HEAD`/ref mtime). Bounded staleness, no correctness change beyond the
   window, and it converts the per-turn cost to once per session burst. (Skipping the fetch
   entirely in world-`all` runs is tempting but wrong to do blind: `--changed` scoping and the
   delta context still derive from the merge-base.)

Not worth taking: the per-file `existsSync`+`statSync` pair and the ~10 git spawns in context
build (42ms total), and pack discovery's eager imports (44ms — load-bearing for structural
discovery, #581).

## 6. Technology review (task 5)

Constraints that frame every verdict: plain Node ≥18, zero dependencies, the engine vendored
verbatim into members, everything must run on credentials and settings members already have. A
tool members must install is dead-on-arrival per the standing ruling (a missing binary = the
capability silently dead per repo); a native-binary npm dependency breaks vendored-verbatim.

### The tools

| Tool | What it is | Verdict for us |
|---|---|---|
| **ESLint v10** | JS linter; since v9.7 a language-agnostic core with official JSON/Markdown/CSS language plugins — rules are `{meta, create}` listeners over a shared parse | Not adoptable (JS-ecosystem dependency tree), but the strongest source of idioms: `meta.messages` with `{{placeholders}}`, `meta.schema` validating per-rule options, capability flags (`fixable`, `hasSuggestions`), RuleTester's valid/invalid contract, and meta-linting rules themselves. Its `no-restricted-syntax` — a generic engine rule instanced by per-config selector+message data — is the field's endorsement of exactly the `patternRule` design (and its findings all reporting one shared rule id is the weakness our per-spec `id` already avoids) |
| **ast-grep** | Rust/tree-sitter structural search; YAML rules (`pattern`/`kind`/`regex` atoms, `inside`/`has` relations, `all`/`any`/`not` composition); Node via `@ast-grep/napi` | **Poor fit.** Our targets are Markdown prose, YAML workflows, JSON configs — Markdown isn't a built-in language (custom grammar = per-platform native artifact), plain text isn't a language at all, and napi is a 0.x native addon resolving nine platform-specific binaries. For config files, path-shaped queries (Spectral) beat CST compositions. Steal the rule-file vocabulary (`id/message/severity/note/fix`, named `utils` sub-rules, the composition algebra) as a future growth path, not the tool |
| **Semgrep** | OCaml/Python semantic grep; `patterns`/`pattern-either`/`pattern-not-inside`, metavariables interpolated into messages; `generic` mode for config-ish text | Non-embeddable (no Node surface; CLI install per member) and the official rules are under an internal-use-only license. Steal: AND/OR/not-inside vocabulary, metavariable-in-message, `focus-metavariable` (match wide, report narrow), per-rule `paths.include/exclude` |
| **remark-lint / markdownlint / textlint** | Markdown/prose linters over mdast / micromark tokens / TxtAST | The dependency trees don't transfer; the contracts do. markdownlint hands every rule both the token stream *and* raw `lines` — endorsement of our line-first engine with an optional structural layer (which `checkSections` already is). Its `fixInfo` (`{lineNumber, editColumn, deleteCount, insertText}` — a fix as a data splice) is the most vendorable autofix model surveyed, the natural shape if declared checks ever grow fixes. Container suppression (ignore matches inside code fences) should be engine-default — `markdownIndex` already blanks fences for sections; line rules don't get that for free yet |
| **Vale** | Go prose linter: styles = directories of YAML rules, each `extends` one of 11 closed primitives (`existence`, `occurrence`, `substitution`, …), with `scope:` targeting document parts (heading/paragraph/list/code) | The closest architectural cousin, independently converged: closed primitive set instantiated by data ≈ the assertion vocabulary; `scope` ≈ `checkSections`. Its `occurrence` primitive (min/max matches in scope) confirms the bounds-cluster merge in §2; single-binary Go distribution confirms there's no free lunch for prose linting as a dependency |
| **Spectral** | Node JSON/YAML linter: `given` (JSONPath) selects nodes, `then` (`field` + function from a small closed set: `pattern`, `truthy`, `defined`, `schema`, `enumeration`, `length`) asserts; `{{path}}`/`{{value}}` message placeholders; `@key` addresses key names | ~20 runtime dependencies — not adoptable. The `given`/`then` decomposition is the model for the parsed-document merge in §2, implementable as a dot-path subset over the existing `fieldAt` + [minimal-yaml](../../engine/checks/helpers/minimal-yaml.mjs) machinery (the YAML half the field solves with heavy parsers, this engine already solved with a vendored minimal one) |
| **actionlint / yamllint** | Deep GitHub-workflow checker (typed `${{ }}` expression checking against modeled contexts) / YAML style checker | actionlint's depth comes from modeling the platform's types — beyond our economics to build, wrong to imitate with regexes. The defensible integration is additive-when-present: a member CI step, or invoked only if the binary exists with an explicit "tool absent, skipped" note (never silent). yamllint: closed rule set, notable only as severity/inline-disable prior art |

### Cross-cutting idioms worth importing

Beyond the ones already folded into §§2–3 (message discipline, meta-lint, named scopes, rule-level
defaults, fixture contract):

- **Dual-tier remediation** — auto-applied `fix` vs human-opted `suggestion`, declared as a
  capability in rule metadata. Relevant only if declared checks grow fixes; if they do,
  markdownlint's data-splice shape keeps the spec pure JSON.
- **Rule tags** for bulk toggling (markdownlint's `headings`/`whitespace`; Semgrep categories).
  At 89 rules with per-pack activation already doing most of that job, not yet earned.
- **`off` as a severity value** — already exists (`rules: {"<id>": "off"}`); the field confirms
  one-knob-per-rule over separate disable mechanisms.
- **Inline disables** (the five-verb `disable`/`enable`/`disable-line`/`disable-next-line`/
  configure-file grammar, with required reasons). The config-side `accept` mechanism with
  mandatory reasons is deliberately stronger (reviewable in one file, provenance-stamped);
  importing inline disables would weaken it. Noted to reject explicitly.
- **A doc URL riding in the finding** (`meta.docs.url`, Vale `link`): the surveyed tools carry
  one; #827 settled that declarations are self-standing, and the message discipline in §3 is how
  that stays workable.

### Embeddability conclusion

Four options weighed: keep the hand-rolled engine (zero install surface, and the hard parts of the
big tools — JS ASTs, taint analysis, typed workflow contexts — are parts this corpus doesn't
need); depend on `@ast-grep/napi` (native 0.x addon, nine platform binaries — breaks
vendored-verbatim for no Markdown/prose payoff); shell out to member-installed CLIs (violates the
runs-on-what-members-have ruling; Semgrep adds a rules-licensing hazard); or adopt formats without
tools. **The last, on top of the first, wins on every axis** — and is what §§2–5 spell out
concretely.

10	// A pack's declarations live in `packs/<pack>/declared-checks.json` (a skill's
11	// in `<pack>/skills/<name>/declared-checks.json`), an array of specs the pack
12	// registry discovers structurally and compiles here into ordinary
13	// `{ id, severity, why, run(ctx) }` rule objects the runner treats like any
14	// other. Nothing wires them: dropping a declaration into the file adds it.
15	//
16	// The format admits no comments — the pattern plus its failureMessage/what/fix
17	// text IS the check — and no prose pointers: a declaration states its own case
18	// or it isn't finished. So a spec carries exactly:
19	//   id              the rule id settings and findings name it by
20	//   severity        'blocking' | 'advisory'
21	//   failureMessage  why this matters, printed on every finding the rule makes
22	//   …the assertions below, each with the `what` and `fix` it fails with
23	//
24	// REGEXES ARE STRINGS in `/body/flags` form — "/^\\s*schedule:/m" — compiled at
25	// load. Keys that accept a path instead (scanFiles, excludeFiles, pathExists)
26	// read any other string as an exact repo path; at every other pattern key a
27	// string that is not in `/…/` form is an authoring error, reported as one.
28	// The engine owns only the walking (the mechanism/policy line line-scanning.mjs
29	// draws): every pattern, file filter, and failure text stays in the declaration.
30	// Spec keys are deliberately wordy — a declaration must read as the whole check
31	// without this header.

34	// the engine makes ONE pass over the scanned tree — each file is read once and
35	// its lines split once, with every subscribing rule's assertions evaluated in
36	// that single visit — and the per-context results are cached, so the first
37	// pattern rule the runner reaches pays for the whole family and the rest are

693	  const { findings, stale } = barrierFindings(ctx, j.spec.edges, j.rule);
694	  const scanErrors = findings.some((f) => f.resolved === undefined);
695	  j.out.push(...(j.spec.fix === undefined ? findings
696	    : findings.map((f) => (f.resolved === undefined ? f : { ...f, fix: j.spec.fix }))));
697	  if (ctx.mode === 'all' && !scanErrors) j.out.push(...staleFindings(stale, j.rule));
698	}
699	
700	// One file visited once for every subscribing rule: whole-text assertions and
701	// repo-wide bookkeeping first, then a single walk of the lines shared by all
702	// the rules' line assertions. A rule with scanIgnoringComments reads the
703	// comment-blanked view of the same file (computed at most once per visit;
704	// stripComments preserves line count, so both views' line numbers agree and
705	// the markdown-section index stays on the raw text).
706	function visit(ctx, subs, path, text) {
707	  let strippedText = null;
708	  const textFor = (j) => (j.spec.scanIgnoringComments ? (strippedText ??= stripComments(text)) : text);
709	  let rawSplit = null;
710	  let strippedSplit = null;
711	  const lines = () => (rawSplit ??= text.split('\n'));
712	  const linesFor = (j) => (j.spec.scanIgnoringComments
713	    ? (strippedSplit ??= textFor(j).split('\n')) : lines());
714	  let mdIndex = null;
715	  const md = () => (mdIndex ??= markdownIndex(text));
716	  const lineJobs = [];
717	
718	  for (const j of subs) {
719	    const s = j.spec;
720	    if (s.checkSections) assertSections(ctx, j, path, md);
721	    if (s.maxLines && lines().length > s.maxLines.limit) {
722	      const vars = { lines: lines().length, limit: s.maxLines.limit };
723	      j.out.push(finding(j.rule, {
724	        file: path, line: s.maxLines.limit + 1,
725	        what: fill(s.maxLines.what, vars), fix: fill(s.maxLines.fix, vars),
726	      }));
727	    }
728	    for (const a of s.checkEachFile ?? []) {
729	      if (a.relevantWhen && !relevant(ctx, a.relevantWhen)) continue;
730	      if (!arr(a.whenFileMatches).every((re) => re.test(textFor(j)))) continue;
731	      if (a.forbid ? a.forbid.test(textFor(j)) : !a.require.test(textFor(j))) {
732	        j.out.push(finding(j.rule, { file: path, what: a.what, fix: a.fix }));
733	      }
734	    }
735	    for (const st of j.repoStates) {
736	      if (st.a.unlessSomeFileMatches.test(textFor(j))) st.satisfied = true;
737	      if (excluded(path, st.a.neverFlagFiles)) continue;
738	      const group = st.a.flagFilesMatching.find((g) => g.every((re) => re.test(textFor(j))));
739	      if (group) {
740	        const at = linesFor(j).findIndex((ln) => group[0].test(ln));
741	        st.hits.push({ file: path, line: at === -1 ? null : at + 1, what: st.a.what, fix: st.a.fix });
742	      }
743	    }
744	    const eligible = (s.matchLines ?? []).filter((a) =>
745	      arr(a.whenFileMatches).every((re) => re.test(textFor(j))) && !a.unlessFileMatches?.test(textFor(j)));
746	    if (eligible.length) lineJobs.push({ j, eligible, viewLines: linesFor(j) });
747	  }
748	
749	  if (!lineJobs.length) return;
750	  for (let i = 0; i < lines().length; i++) {
751	    for (const { j, eligible, viewLines } of lineJobs) {
752	      const ln = viewLines[i];
753	      if (j.spec.skipLinesMatching?.test(ln)) continue;
754	      for (const a of eligible) {
755	        const m = ln.match(a.match);
756	        if (!m || a.unlessLineMatches?.test(ln)) continue;
757	        const vars = { match: m[0] };
758	        j.out.push(finding(j.rule, {
759	          file: path, line: i + 1, what: fill(a.what, vars), fix: fill(a.fix, vars),
760	        }));
761	        break;
762	      }
763	    }
764	  }
765	}
766	
767	function results(ctx) {
768	  let res = scans.get(ctx);
769	  if (res) return res;
770	  res = new Map();
771	  scans.set(ctx, res);
772	
773	  const jobs = [];
774	  for (const rule of REGISTRY) {
775	    const out = [];
776	    res.set(rule, out);
777	    if (!relevant(ctx, rule.spec.relevantWhen)) continue;
778	    jobs.push({
779	      rule, spec: rule.spec, out,
780	      repoStates: (rule.spec.repoWide ?? []).map((a) => ({ a, satisfied: false, hits: [] })),
781	    });
782	  }
783	
784	  const parsedDocs = new Map();
785	  const parsed = (path) => {
786	    if (!parsedDocs.has(path)) {
787	      const text = ctx.read(path);
788	      let doc = null;
789	      if (text !== null) {
790	        if (/\.ya?ml$/.test(path)) doc = parseYaml(text);
791	        else { try { doc = JSON.parse(text); } catch { doc = null; } }
792	      }
793	      parsedDocs.set(path, doc);
794	    }
795	    return parsedDocs.get(path);
796	  };
797	
798	  for (const j of jobs) {
799	    assertTreeShape(ctx, j);
800	    assertParsedShape(ctx, j, parsed);
801	    if (j.spec.edges) assertReferenceEdges(ctx, j);
802	    if (typeof j.spec.scanFiles !== 'string') continue;
803	    const text = ctx.read(j.spec.scanFiles);
804	    if (text === null) {
805	      if (j.spec.whenMissing) {
806	        j.out.push(finding(j.rule, { file: j.spec.scanFiles, what: j.spec.whenMissing.what, fix: j.spec.whenMissing.fix }));
807	      }
808	      continue;
809	    }
810	    visit(ctx, [j], j.spec.scanFiles, text);
811	  }
812	
813	  const swept = jobs.filter((j) => j.spec.scanMatchers.length);
814	  if (swept.length) {
815	    const scanned = new Set(ctx.files);
816	    const tracked = new Set(ctx.tracked);
817	    for (const path of [...ctx.files, ...ctx.tracked.filter((f) => !scanned.has(f))]) {
818	      const subs = swept.filter((j) =>
819	        (j.spec.scanTracked ? tracked : scanned).has(path) &&
820	        j.spec.scanMatchers.some((re) => re.test(path)) && !excluded(path, j.spec.excludeMatchers));
821	      if (!subs.length) continue;
822	      const text = ctx.read(path);
823	      if (text !== null) visit(ctx, subs, path, text);
824	    }
825	  }
826	
827	  for (const j of jobs) {
828	    for (const st of j.repoStates) {
829	      if (!st.satisfied) for (const h of st.hits) j.out.push(finding(j.rule, h));
830	    }
831	    const marker = j.spec.relevantWhen?.repoContains;
832	    if (marker && j.out.length &&
833	        !ctx.files.some((f) => !excluded(f, j.spec.excludeMatchers) && marker.test(ctx.read(f) ?? ''))) {
834	      j.out.length = 0;
835	    }
836	  }
837	  return res;
838	}
839	
840	// Where a declaration says RegExp: keys reading `/body/flags` strings. The two
841	// sets differ in what a NON-regex string means — a path at PATH_OR_PATTERN_KEYS
842	// (scanFiles: "README.md" is read directly), an authoring error anywhere else.
843	const PATH_OR_PATTERN_KEYS = new Set(['scanFiles', 'excludeFiles']);
844	const PATTERN_KEYS = new Set([
845	  'skipLinesMatching', 'match', 'unlessLineMatches', 'whenFileMatches', 'unlessFileMatches',
846	  'require', 'forbid', 'trackedFileMatches', 'noTrackedFileMatches', 'exactlyOneTrackedFileMatches',
847	  'pathMatching', 'text', 'repoContains', 'unlessSomeFileMatches', 'flagFilesMatching',
848	  'neverFlagFiles', 'eachTrackedPathMatching', 'eachPathMatching', 'globLineMatching',
849	  'filesMatching', 'whereFileContains', 'inFilesMatching', 'pattern',
850	  'eachScannedPathMatching', 'coveredByGlobLinesMatching',
851	]);
852	const RE_FORM = /^\/(.*)\/([dgimsuvy]*)$/s;
853	
854	// Compile a spec's pattern strings in place of their keys, leaving every other
855	// value (paths, field names, failure text, numbers) exactly as declared. A real
856	// RegExp passes through, so a spec built in code — the engine's own tests — is
857	// the same object either way.
858	function compileSpec(value, key, where) {
859	  if (Array.isArray(value)) return value.map((v) => compileSpec(v, key, where));
860	  if (value === null || value instanceof RegExp) return value;
861	  if (typeof value === 'string') {
862	    if (!PATTERN_KEYS.has(key) && !PATH_OR_PATTERN_KEYS.has(key)) return value;
863	    const form = RE_FORM.exec(value);
864	    if (!form) {
865	      if (PATH_OR_PATTERN_KEYS.has(key)) return value;
866	      throw new Error(`${where}: "${key}" takes a regex in /pattern/flags form, not ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
867	    }
868	    try { return new RegExp(form[1], form[2]); }
869	    catch (e) { throw new Error(`${where}: "${key}" is not a valid regex — ${e.message}`); }
870	  }
871	  if (typeof value !== 'object') return value;
872	  const out = {};
873	  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(value)) out[k] = compileSpec(v, k, where);
874	  return out;
875	}
876	
877	export function patternRule(declaration, { selfExclude = null } = {}) {
878	  const where = `the declared check "${declaration.id}"`;
879	  if (typeof declaration.id !== 'string' || !declaration.id.trim()) {
880	    throw new Error('a declared check needs a non-empty "id"');
881	  }
882	  if (declaration.severity !== 'blocking' && declaration.severity !== 'advisory') {
883	    throw new Error(`${where}: severity must be "blocking" or "advisory", not ${JSON.stringify(declaration.severity)}`);
884	  }
885	  validateSpecKeys(declaration, 'spec', where);
886	  const spec = compileSpec(declaration, null, where);
887	  normalizeLegacySpellings(spec);
888	  validateMergedEntries(spec, where);
889	  const classPatterns = (names) => (names ?? []).map((n) => {
890	    if (!FILE_CLASSES[n]) {
891	      throw new Error(`${where}: "${n}" is not a file class — the classes are: ${Object.keys(FILE_CLASSES).join(', ')}`);
892	    }
893	    return FILE_CLASSES[n];
894	  });
895	  const scanClasses = classPatterns(spec.scanFileClasses);
896	  if (scanClasses.length && typeof spec.scanFiles === 'string') {
897	    throw new Error(`${where}: scanFileClasses cannot combine with an exact-path scanFiles`);
898	  }
899	  // The normalized selection surface the scan reads: the sweep patterns
900	  // (regex scanFiles + classes) and every exclusion (declared, class-named,
901	  // and the loader-supplied self-exclusion) as flat lists.
902	  spec.scanMatchers = [...(spec.scanFiles instanceof RegExp ? [spec.scanFiles] : []), ...scanClasses];
903	  spec.excludeMatchers = [
904	    ...(spec.excludeFiles != null ? [spec.excludeFiles] : []),
905	    ...classPatterns(spec.excludeFileClasses),
906	    ...(selfExclude ? [selfExclude] : []),
907	  ];
908	  if (typeof spec.fix === 'string') applyFixDefault(spec, spec.fix);
909	  if (spec.forbidReferences !== undefined) {
910	    const { edges, errors } = normalizeEdges(spec.forbidReferences);
911	    if (errors.length) throw new Error(`${where}: ${errors[0].what} — ${errors[0].fix}`);
912	    spec.edges = edges;
913	  }
914	  const rule = {
915	    id: spec.id,
916	    severity: spec.severity,
917	    why: spec.failureMessage,
918	    spec,
919	    run(ctx) { return results(ctx).get(rule); },
920	  };
921	  REGISTRY.push(rule);
922	  return rule;
923	}
924	
925	// A directory's declared checks: `<dir>/declared-checks.json`, an array of specs
926	// compiled into rules — none when the file is absent. Cached by path, so the
927	// registry and a test asking the same directory share one set of rule objects
928	// (two would each re-run the shared scan for the same assertions).
929	//
930	// A SKILL's declarations (a dir named `…/skills/<name>`) are compiled with a
931	// structural self-exclusion — content under any `skills/<name>/` path segment
932	// pair is out of every assertion's scope — so a skill's own SKILL.md examples
933	// never trip its checks, in whichever tree the skill's content appears (the
934	// canon's packs/<pack>/skills/, a root skills/ layout, a consumer's mounted
935	// .claude/skills/ links), without each declaration hand-spelling the exclusion.
936	const loaded = new Map();
937	export function loadDeclaredChecks(dir) {
938	  const path = join(dir, 'declared-checks.json');
939	  if (!loaded.has(path)) {
940	    let specs = [];
941	    if (existsSync(path)) {
942	      let raw;
943	      try { raw = JSON.parse(readFileSync(path, 'utf8')); }
944	      catch (e) { throw new Error(`${path} is not valid JSON: ${e.message}`); }
945	      if (!Array.isArray(raw)) throw new Error(`${path} must be an array of check declarations`);
946	      specs = raw;
947	    }
948	    const skillName = /(^|[\\/])skills[\\/]([^\\/]+)$/.exec(dir)?.[2];
949	    const selfExclude = skillName ? new RegExp(`(^|/)skills/${escapeRe(skillName)}/`) : null;
950	    loaded.set(path, specs.map((s) => patternRule(s, { selfExclude })));
951	  }
952	  return loaded.get(path);
953	}

input.title: Declarative checks: fence-blind markdown scanning and a line-count bounds assertion
input.body:
Owner-approved follow-up to the declarative-checks review (#838, merged in #839): implement the first two redesign recommendations.

1. **Fence-blind markdown scanning** — `scanIgnoringMarkdownFences: true`: content assertions read each markdown file with fenced code blocks blanked (line count preserved), the view `checkSections` already gets via `markdownIndex`, so an example inside a fence never satisfies or trips a pattern.
2. **Line-count bounds** — `countMatchingLines: [{ linesMatching, atLeast, atMost, what, fix }]`: per scanned file, the number of matching lines must sit within the declared bounds (Vale's `occurrence` idiom; the count form of the bounds cluster in `docs/declarative-checks/REVIEW.md` §2).

Also in this change: survey of candidates for `@key` addressing and declarative autofix (analysis only, reported in session).

input.title: Fence-blind markdown scanning and line-count bounds in the declarative vocabulary
input.head: claude/declarative-checks-review-tdg3by
input.body:
Implements the first two owner-approved redesign recommendations from the declarative-checks review (#838/#839). Closes #843.

- **`scanIgnoringMarkdownFences: true`** — content assertions (`matchLines`, `checkEachFile`, `repoWide`, `countMatchingLines`) read each markdown file with fenced code blocks blanked, line count preserved: the same view `checkSections` always had via `markdownIndex` (the fence pass is now the shared `blankMarkdownFences`). Non-markdown files are untouched, so a mixed scan stays honest. First customer: `cer/readme-sections` — a `## Install` heading shown inside a fenced example no longer satisfies its `require`.
- **`countMatchingLines: [{ linesMatching, atLeast, atMost, what, fix }]`** — per scanned file, the number of matching lines must sit within the declared bounds (Vale's `occurrence` idiom). `atMost: 0` forbids the pattern; too many anchors at the first line past the bound, too few at the file; `{count}`/`{atLeast}`/`{atMost}` interpolate. Bounds are validated at load (pattern required, at least one bound, whole numbers, `atLeast ≤ atMost`) so a boundless entry cannot silently assert nothing. Counting respects the rule's `scanIgnoring*` view. First conversion customer arrives with `scheduler-workflow-shape`'s cron legs (tracked in #838).

The two `scanIgnoring*` keys now compose through one memoized per-visit view map instead of ad-hoc single-view caching. Five new engine tests, written red-first; full suite 1679/1679, both sweeps clean.
